Technical Guide

PTFE vs PEEK: Which Polymer When?

Both are high-performance polymers that survive heat and aggressive chemicals, but they solve very different engineering problems. Here is how they compare.

PTFE and PEEK often appear on the same shortlist: both run at around 250 °C, both resist a wide range of chemicals, and both are used for seals, valve seats, bushes and insulators. In practice they are rarely interchangeable. PTFE is soft, slippery and almost chemically inert; PEEK is strong, stiff and dimensionally stable. Choosing between them starts with asking which of those qualities your part actually needs.

Side-by-side comparison

Typical literature values for unfilled grades, for comparison only. Filled grades of both materials differ significantly — confirm data for the specific grade.
PropertyPTFE (virgin)PEEK (unfilled)
Density2.14–2.20 g/cm³approx. 1.3 g/cm³
Tensile strengthapprox. 20–35 MPaapprox. 90–100 MPa
Tensile modulusapprox. 0.4–0.75 GPaapprox. 3.5–4 GPa
Creep under sustained loadHigh (cold flow)Low
Coefficient of frictionapprox. 0.05–0.10 dynamic on steel — among the lowest of any solidConsiderably higher; bearing grades are modified with PTFE, graphite or carbon fibre
Continuous service temperatureapprox. −200 °C to +260 °Capprox. 250 °C (upper)
Melting pointapprox. 327 °C (very high melt viscosity — does not flow readily)approx. 343 °C
Chemical resistanceResists virtually all industrial chemicalsVery good, but attacked by concentrated sulphuric acid and some strong oxidisers
Hot water and steamUnaffectedGood hydrolysis resistance
Ionising radiationPoorGood
Dielectric constantapprox. 2.1, very stableHigher than PTFE
ProcessingCompression moulded and sintered, then machinedMelt-processable: injection moulded, extruded or machined
Relative material costLowerConsiderably higher

The pattern is consistent: PEEK wins on mechanical performance, dimensional stability and radiation resistance; PTFE wins on friction, chemical inertness, low-temperature toughness, electrical properties and cost. Temperature, often the first thing people check, is rarely the deciding factor, because both materials have similar upper limits.

Strength, stiffness and creep

This is the biggest difference. Unfilled PEEK has roughly three to four times the tensile strength of PTFE and is around five to ten times as stiff. It holds its shape under sustained load, resists extrusion into clearance gaps and can carry structural loads in a way PTFE cannot.

PTFE’s low stiffness and tendency to creep are a weakness for structural parts but an advantage for sealing: it conforms to the mating surface at low contact stress. Fillers narrow the gap — filled PTFE grades resist creep much better than virgin — but even heavily filled PTFE does not approach PEEK’s stiffness.

One nuance: PEEK’s glass transition sits at roughly 140–145 °C. Above it PEEK remains useful, but its stiffness falls noticeably, so its advantage over PTFE is largest at moderate temperatures.

Friction and wear

PTFE has one of the lowest coefficients of friction of any solid (approximately 0.05–0.10 dynamic against steel), with no stick–slip. Unfilled PEEK’s friction is considerably higher. For sliding and bearing service, PEEK is normally used as a “bearing grade” modified with PTFE, graphite and carbon fibre — which is itself a sign of how valuable PTFE’s lubricity is.

On wear, the picture reverses: virgin PTFE wears quickly under load, while PEEK and its bearing grades handle much higher pressures and speeds. Filled PTFE sits between the two.

Temperature range

Both materials have upper continuous service limits in the same region — about 260 °C for PTFE and about 250 °C for PEEK. The differences are elsewhere:

  • At low temperature, PTFE stays tough and flexible down to cryogenic temperatures, which is why it is common in cryogenic seals and valve seats.
  • At high temperature under load, PEEK keeps far more of its strength, while PTFE creeps faster as temperature rises.
  • Dimensionally, PTFE has a high thermal expansion and a crystalline transition near 19 °C; PEEK expands less and has no such room-temperature transition.

Chemical, hydrolysis and radiation resistance

PTFE is the more chemically resistant of the two. Virgin PTFE resists virtually all industrial chemicals; the exceptions are molten or dissolved alkali metals, elemental fluorine and chlorine trifluoride, and swelling in some halogenated compounds at high temperature (see our chemical resistance guide). PEEK has very good resistance to most chemicals, but it is attacked by concentrated sulphuric acid and some strong oxidising agents.

Both handle hot water and steam well; PEEK’s hydrolysis resistance is one reason it is used in repeatedly steam-sterilised components.

Radiation is where PEEK clearly wins. PTFE has poor resistance to ionising radiation and becomes brittle at relatively low doses; PEEK tolerates radiation well. For nuclear service or gamma-sterilised parts, PEEK is usually the better choice.

Electrical properties

Both are good insulators. PTFE has the lower and more stable dielectric constant (approximately 2.1) and very low dielectric loss, so it is preferred for high-frequency insulation, RF connectors and cable dielectrics. PEEK is chosen where an insulator must also be strong and stiff — structural insulating parts, terminal blocks and connectors that carry mechanical load.

Processing and part manufacture

PEEK is melt-processable. It can be injection moulded, which makes high-volume, complex parts economical once a mould exists, and it can also be extruded and machined from stock.

PTFE is not melt-processable. It is compression moulded and sintered into sheets, rods, tubes and billets, and finished parts are machined from that stock or cut from sheet. This favours prototypes, low and medium volumes, and large or simple shapes, with no mould cost — but complex parts in high volume can cost more to machine than to mould.

Cost

PEEK is considerably more expensive than PTFE as a raw material. The gap narrows somewhat when comparing by volume, because PEEK is much less dense (about 1.3 g/cm³ against roughly 2.2 g/cm³ for PTFE), and part cost also depends on machining time and quantity. Even so, specifying PEEK where PTFE would do the job adds cost without benefit — and vice versa, using PTFE where PEEK is needed leads to early failures that cost more than the material saving.

When to use each

Choose PTFE when

  • the media is highly aggressive or not fully defined;
  • you need the lowest friction, non-stick behaviour or smooth stick–slip-free motion;
  • the part seals by conforming — gaskets, seals and seat inserts at modest loads;
  • the service extends to cryogenic temperatures;
  • high-frequency electrical performance matters;
  • cost matters and the mechanical demands are modest.

Choose PEEK when

  • the part carries structural or sustained load, or must hold close tolerances at temperature;
  • creep or extrusion would defeat PTFE, for example high-pressure valve seats and back-up rings;
  • the part sees ionising radiation or radiation sterilisation;
  • high volumes justify injection moulding a complex shape.

Consider combining them

Many good designs use both: a PEEK body or back-up ring to carry load and prevent extrusion, with a PTFE seal or seat face to provide sealing and low friction. Filled PTFE is also worth evaluating before moving to PEEK — it often resolves creep and wear problems at lower cost.
